messages.subject: hypothesis testing of negative_binomial data
parts:
Hello Community,

I would like to do a hypothesis testing for count over-dispersed data using negative binomial (NB). As far as I am aware I have two options

1) model comparison, under two conditions -> H0 observations come from one NB; and H1 observations come from two NB

The problem is that I don;t have 1 comparison but many. So I cannot use a global probability value because I need to provide H0 of H1 for every comparison

2) I have been suggested here to use generated quantities to observe how likely if that a value is bigger than another



generated quantities {
    int<lower=0, upper=1> comparison [G];
 
  for(g in 1:G) comparison[g] = mu[1,g] > mu[2,g];
}




However when I place an hyper-prior on the two means to be compared, the model stop converging



data {
int<lower=1> G; // number of genes
int<lower=1> S; // number of samples
int y[S,G]; // data. gene expression (integer counts)
int c[S]; // mapping samples - treatment 1 and 2
}
parameters {
vector<lower=0>[G] mu[2]; // prior location mu_mean; // prior location mu_sd; // prior location
real<lower=0> phi;  // Over-dispersion
vector<lower=0>[G] mu_mean;
vector<lower=0>[G] mu_sd;
}
model {

phi ~ normal(0,4);
for(s in 1:S) y[s] ~ neg_binomial_2( mu[c[s]], phi );


//-----------------------------------------------------------------//
// There are just two numbers to predict each of mu_mean and mu_sd //
//-----------------------------------------------------------------//

for(i in 1:2) mu[i] ~ normal(mu_mean, mu_sd );

//-----------------------------------------------------------------//

mu_sd ~ lognormal(4, 2); // hyperprior
    mu_mean ~ lognormal(6, 3); //hyperprior
}
generated quantities {
int<lower=0, upper=1> comparison [G];
for(g in 1:G) comparison[g] = mu[1,g] > mu[2,g];
}





Thanks a lot!

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] hypothesis testing of negative_binomial data
parts:
For (1) I don't understand how you're trying to run a hypothesis test with
Bayesian inference.

For (2), why change the priors if you're going to compare parameters? I'd
suggest fitting the model, then adding the generated quantities.

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] hypothesis testing of negative_binomial data
parts:
Thanks Bob for the answer,

1. I agree it is a bit strange. After I calculate quantity 1 and 2 for many G entities, I have to answer the question are 1 and 2 for each of G entities coming from two distributions or one. Since all parameters are in the same model I cannot compare the model globally, a solution the community suggested was to use generated quantities for achieving that.

2. Sorry I am not sure what prior in particular you are referring to? Are you saying I should not use hyper-priors mu_mean and mu_sd?

Thanks a lot

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] hypothesis testing of negative_binomial data
parts:
> On Mar 29, 2017, at 11:53 PM, stefano <mangiol...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> Thanks Bob for the answer,
>
> 1. I agree it is a bit strange. After I calculate quantity 1 and 2 for many G entities, I have to answer the question are 1 and 2 for each of G entities coming from two distributions or one. Since all parameters are in the same model I cannot compare the model globally, a solution the community suggested was to use generated quantities for achieving that.
>
> 2. Sorry I am not sure what prior in particular you are referring to? Are you saying I should not use hyper-priors mu_mean and mu_sd?

I meant fit the model without the generated quantities first. They're
not going to change your fit. Get the fit right, then add generated
quantities.

We're going to develop a way to run generated quantities after the main
fit soon, so that should help with some of this workflow complexity.

- Bob
